title: The doctor & pharmacy
intro:
For everyday illness, go to a local clinic ({クリニック} or {医院[いいん]}) rather than a big hospital. Clinics are organized by specialty: {内科[ないか]} (internal medicine, for colds, fever and stomach trouble), {耳鼻科[じびか]} (ear, nose and throat), {皮膚科[ひふか]} (skin), {整形外科[せいけいげか]} (bones, joints and injuries), {歯科[しか]} (dentist). Large hospitals often expect a referral letter ({紹介状[しょうかいじょう]}) and may charge an extra fee without one.

Bring proof of health insurance. Japan has been moving health insurance onto the My Number card, so many clinics now have a card reader at reception; if you have a different insurance document, bring that. With public insurance, most working-age adults pay a share of the cost (commonly 30%) at the counter. Some small clinics still accept only cash.

On your first visit ({初診[しょしん]}) you will fill in a questionnaire ({問診票[もんしんひょう]}) about your symptoms, allergies and current medication. Ask for an English version if there is one, or prepare your answers in advance with a translation app.

The doctor gives you a prescription ({処方箋[しょほうせん]}), which you take to a pharmacy ({薬局[やっきょく]}), often right next to the clinic. The pharmacist explains how to take the medicine and may offer a medication notebook ({お薬[くすり]手帳[てちょう]}) that records your prescriptions. Over-the-counter medicine is sold at drugstores. Note that some medicines common abroad are restricted in Japan; check official guidance before bringing medicine with you.

phrases.jp: 初[はじ]めてなんですが、診[み]ていただけますか。
phrases.en: It's my first time here. Could I see a doctor?

phrases.jp: マイナンバーカードを保険証[ほけんしょう]として使[つか]えますか。
phrases.en: Can I use my My Number card as my insurance card?

phrases.jp: 頭[あたま]が痛[いた]いです。
喉[のど]が痛[いた]くて、咳[せき]が出[で]ます。
phrases.en: My throat hurts and I have a cough.

phrases.jp: 昨日[きのう]から下痢[げり]が続[つづ]いています。
三日前[みっかまえ]からです。
ペニシリンにアレルギーがあります。
今[いま]、飲[の]んでいる薬[くすり]はありません。
phrases.en: I'm not taking any medication right now.

phrases.jp: 英語[えいご]が話[はな]せる先生[せんせい]はいますか。
phrases.en: Is there a doctor who speaks English?

phrases.jp: 診断書[しんだんしょ]を書[か]いていただけますか。
phrases.en: Could you write me a medical certificate?
phrases.note: Some employers ask for one if you are off sick for several days. There is usually a fee.

phrases.jp: この薬[くすり]は一日[いちにち]何回[なんかい]飲[の]みますか。
phrases.en: How many times a day do I take this medicine?

phrases.jp: 食後[しょくご]に飲[の]んでください。
飲[の]むと眠[ねむ]くなりますか。
風邪薬[かぜぐすり]はどこにありますか。

vocab.jp: 問診票[もんしんひょう]
お薬[くすり]手帳[てちょう]
紹介状[しょうかいじょう]

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.jp: こんにちは。今日[きょう]はどうされましたか。
dialogue.en: Hello. What brings you in today?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: 熱[ねつ]と咳[せき]があって、診[み]ていただきたいんですが。
dialogue.en: I have a fever and a cough, and I'd like to see the doctor.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.jp: こちらは初[はじ]めてですか。
dialogue.en: Is this your first visit here?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.jp: では、保険証[ほけんしょう]かマイナンバーカードをお願[ねが]いします。こちらの問診票[もんしんひょう]にご記入[きにゅう]ください。
dialogue.en: Then your insurance card or My Number card, please. And please fill in this questionnaire.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.jp: いつから熱[ねつ]がありますか。
dialogue.en: Since when have you had the fever?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: 一昨日[おととい]の夜[よる]からです。

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.jp: 喉[のど]が少[すこ]し赤[あか]いですね。風邪[かぜ]だと思[おも]います。お薬[くすり]を出[だ]しておきますね。
dialogue.en: Your throat is a little red. I think it's a cold. I'll prescribe some medicine.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: 仕事[しごと]は休[やす]んだほうがいいですか。
dialogue.en: Should I take time off work?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.jp: 熱[ねつ]が下[さ]がるまでは、休[やす]んでください。
dialogue.en: Please rest until the fever goes down.

tips: Check clinic opening hours online before going. Many close for a long lunch break, on Sundays, and on one weekday afternoon.
Use your medication notebook ({お薬[くすり]手帳[てちょう]}) or its app version every time; it helps pharmacists avoid dangerous combinations.
Before moving to Japan, check the official rules on bringing medicine. Some stimulant-based medicines that are legal elsewhere are prohibited, and larger quantities may need advance paperwork.
Write down your symptoms, when they started and any allergies in Japanese before you go. Showing a note is perfectly acceptable.
Keep receipts for medical costs. If your household's medical spending is high in a year, you may be able to claim a tax deduction.
